description: No Bribri or Cabécar source documents a serpent called 'La Culebra Mayor' ('The Greater Snake'). Talamancan mythology does preserve great serpents under other names: ChbekoL, a giant snake that devoured those who broke the incest laws, and Dululba, a snake of justice. The entry's claims of an association with Sibö and the creation of landforms are unattested inventions.
source: Review finding: unattested as named; genuine Talamancan serpents are ChbekoL and Dululba (Talamancan mythology, Bribri/Cabécar tradition).
research_notes: Marked unattested. No 'La Culebra Mayor' in Bribri/Cabécar sources; the genuine serpent figures are ChbekoL (punisher of incest) and Dululba, plus the two-headed Jala Jala. Description corrected to the attested tradition.

description: 'La Trola' appears only in a single AI-generated Miskito story retelling online; no Nicaraguan folklore source or ethnographic record documents this named figure. Genuine Miskito water-beliefs center on other beings, and Nicaragua's coastal tradition knows figures such as the Cegua and Wihwin-type water spirits, but 'La Trola' has no attestation.

research_notes: Marked unattested: sole source is an AI-style content retelling. The input's Wihwin derivation is speculative; description corrected to note genuine Miskito coastal spirit lore without the fabricated figure.

description: El Tabudo ('Man of Big Knees') is a water-spirit or lake-guardian of Salvadoran folklore tied to Lake Coatepeque in Santa Ana department. Legend says a rich lakeside landowner was dragged beneath the water and returned months later transformed, with swollen knees and a fish-like appearance; he now haunts the lake, sometimes appearing as a fisherman to lure people in.
source: Salvadoran oral tradition; documented on walkingwithelsalvador.org and Salvadoran legend roundups (Guanacos, El Salvador Tips).
research_notes: Verified attested. El Tabudo is a genuine Lake Coatepeque legend; kept the core narrative (wealthy man transformed, swollen knees), trimmed invented conservation-moral framing. Attested.

description: The Gulyabani is a ghoul-like being of Turkish and Anatolian folk belief, from Persian 'Gul-i Beyabani' ('desert ghoul'). It haunts graveyards, ruins, and lonely roads at night, preying on travelers and those who wander alone after dark. In Turkish tradition it appears as a bogeyman used to keep children indoors, and it features in classical Turkish literature.
source: Turkish folklore and literary tradition; Persian-derived name (gul-i biyabani), documented in Turkish folk-belief surveys.
research_notes: Verified attested: Gulyabani is a genuine Turkish/Anatolian ghoul-like figure (gul-i biyabani). Description grounded; removed template filler and unverified film claims.

description: The Karakoncolos is a winter demon of Turkish and Balkan folk belief, known in the Black Sea and northeastern Anatolia and among Bulgarian, Serbian, and Greek neighbors as Karakondžula or similar names. It is said to appear in the coldest midwinter days, imitating human voices to lure people outdoors into the freezing dark. Parents invoked it to keep children indoors at night.
source: Turkish and Balkan folk tradition; documented in regional demonology surveys (Karakondžula/Kallikantzaros parallels).
research_notes: Verified attested: Karakoncolos (Karakondžula) is a genuine winter bogey. Description trimmed and grounded; removed unverified '40 days Zemheri' precision and fire-element claim.

description: Swaichen (also spelled Swaychen) is a sea-creature of Bahraini folklore that punishes those who steal from the sea, taking from the water without respect. In a 2022 Gulf Weekly feature, Bahraini artist Zainab Almahdi presented it as a towering figure rising from the water that reclaims the thief; the tale is offered as a modern retelling of a traditional maritime warning legend.
source: Gulf Weekly (April 2022), 'Myths and legends given shape'; Bahraini oral tradition on sea folklore; artist Zainab Almahdi's 'What Belongs to the Sea'.
research_notes: Attested, thinly. The named creature is documented mainly through contemporary Bahraini retellings (Gulf Weekly, artist Zainab Almahdi) grounded in maritime folklore about respecting the sea; kept attested with a cautious, source-faithful description.

description: The Tantal (Arabic 'tanṭāl') is a shapeshifting being of Iraqi folklore, particularly among the Marsh Arabs of southern Iraq. It can appear as a human, animal, or object and is active at night; specific Tantals are associated with particular marsh territories, and one, Tantal Hafiz, is named as a chief of them. The figure is documented in Iraqi oral tradition and journalism.
source: Iraqi Marsh Arab oral tradition; documented by Abdulrahman Zeyad (Al Jazeera, 2023) and Drower, 'Folk-Tales of Iraq'.
research_notes: Verified attested: Tantal is a documented Iraqi shapeshifting being. Kept core facts (territory-specific Tantals, Tantal Hafiz); trimmed 'guardian of treasure' and prophecy claims as unverified. Note: duplicates tantal-iraq and tantal-kuwait entries.

description: The Tantal is a shapeshifting spirit of Iraqi folklore, tied especially to the marshlands of southern Iraq and the Marsh Arab (Ma'dan) communities. It is said to change shape at night, appearing as a human, animal, or object, and particular Tantals are named for the marsh territories they haunt, with Tantal Hafiz regarded as foremost among them. Documented in Drower's Folk-Tales of Iraq.
source: Iraqi folklore; E. S. Drower, 'Folk-Tales of Iraq' (1931); modern journalistic accounts of Tantal belief.
research_notes: Verified attested. This entry duplicates 'tantal' (same figure, Iraqi origin); kept with corrected description and flagged as a merge candidate. Attested.

description: The Tantal is a shapeshifting being of the southern Mesopotamian marshlands, documented among the Marsh Arabs; in Gulf usage the figure also appears in Kuwaiti retellings. It shifts between human, animal, and object forms at night, and individual Tantals are named for the territories they haunt, with Tantal Hafiz described as their ruler. The core lore is Iraqi; the Kuwait framing is derivative.

research_notes: Attested as the same Tantal figure; Kuwait attribution is derivative of the Iraqi origin. Description corrected, noted as duplicate of 'tantal'/'tantal-iraq'; merge candidate.

description: Umm Al Duwais ('Mother of the Toes') is a female jinn of Gulf Arab folklore, celebrated in Emirati and Bahraini tradition. She appears as a beautiful, perfumed woman who lures men near deserted places, then turns monstrous. Her legend is recorded in Gulf oral tradition and has inspired modern films and retellings. This entry duplicates the United Arab Emirates variant of the same figure.
source: Gulf Arab folklore; documented in Emirati and Bahraini sources and contemporary features (The National, Gulf retellings).
research_notes: Verified attested: Umm Al Duwais is a documented Gulf female jinn. Duplicates ummalduwais-unitedarabemirates; description written for the shared figure, noted as merge candidate. Attested.

description: Umm Al Duwais ('Mother of the Toes') is the best-known female jinn of Emirati folklore, rooted in Bedouin oral tradition. She appears as a beautiful woman in gold and perfume who approaches men straying after dark near abandoned buildings, date groves, or desert roads, charms them, then reveals her monstrous form. The 2013 film 'Djinn' (Tobe Hooper) drew on the legend.
source: Emirati oral tradition; The National news features; contemporary Emirati folklore accounts.
research_notes: Verified attested and well-documented. Description grounded in attested details; removed the awkward appended sentence from the input. Attested.

description: 'Akkarmora' is not attested in Norwegian folklore. Web research and Norwegian folk-belief records show no sea-guardian of this name; the entry appears invented from 'akkar' (Norwegian for squid/octopus) plus 'mora' (mother). Genuine Nordic sea beliefs include the Kraken and the hafgufa, and the draug of the sea, but no Måsøy 'squid mother' legend is documented.

research_notes: Marked unattested: no source documents 'Akkarmora'; name is a plausible-sounding coinage from Norwegian words. Genuine analogues noted (Kraken/hafgufa, sea-draug). Description corrected.

description: Dønnamannen ('the Man of Dønna') is a troll of Norwegian legend tied to the reclining rock formation on the island of Dønna in Nordland. The story connects him to the Seven Sisters, the famous mountain range on nearby Alstenøya: as a troll he is said to have been turned to stone, and his rock silhouette lies on its back with hands folded across its chest, visible from the sea.
source: Norwegian regional legend and place-name tradition of Helgeland (Nordland); folklore and tourism accounts of Dønnamannen.
research_notes: Verified attested: Dønnamannen is a genuine Dønna rock-formation legend linked to the Seven Sisters. Description grounded in the attested landform story; removed the moralizing 'cautionary tale' framing.

description: A dradokke (dra-doll, dragedokke) is a doll-like object of Norwegian folk belief that 'draws' wealth to its owner. Sources in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling record that it was sent out at night to bring back milk, grain, clothes, gold, and silver, sometimes from drowned men at the seabed; recipes for making one could call for stolen cloth or a dead thief's right thumb.
source: Norwegian folk belief; Norsk Folkeminnesamling records; Ørnulf Hodne, 'Vetter og skrømt' (1995); SAMLA/Universitetet i Bergen; Bø 1987.
research_notes: Verified attested: dradokke is a documented Norwegian folk-magic object (wealth-drawing doll, akin to trollkatt). Rewrote from primary material; removed invented remedies (burning) and builder's-offering claims.

description: Draugur (Faroese dreygur) is the Faroese form of the Norse draugr, a walking dead being of island tradition. Draugar in the Faroes were often described as large figures in grey clothes who guarded burial mounds and treasure or, in sea lore, as the drowned dead who rose to drag the living down. The sign of the cross and naming them aloud were said to ward them off.
source: Faroese oral tradition; recorded in Nordic folklore collections on the draugr/revenant motif.
research_notes: Verified attested: the Faroese draugur is the local draugr/revenant, well grounded in island folk belief. Description corrected; removed the unsupported 'similar to Huldufólk' comparison.

description: Gruvrået, also called Gruvfrun or Gruvjungfrun, is the guardian spirit of mines in Swedish folklore, especially in the Bergslagen mining district. She is said to walk the tunnels as an elegantly dressed woman with a ring of keys; her dress color was read as an omen, and she rewarded respectful miners with rich ore while punishing swearing and careless behavior in the workings.
source: Swedish folk belief; ethnographic records of Bergslagen mining tradition on the gruvrå/mine spirit.
research_notes: Verified attested: gruvrå/gruvrået is a documented Swedish mine spirit. Description grounded in attested dress-omen and offering beliefs; trimmed and focused.

description: Helhest ('Hell-horse') is the three-legged horse of Danish folk belief, a death-omen that haunted churchyards. It was said to drag itself around the church at night, and whoever saw it or heard it whinny would die within the year. Old accounts tie the creature to a horse or sacrificial beast buried alive beneath a church or graveyard; stories cluster at Aarhus, Roskilde, and other towns.
source: Danish folk tradition; documented in Danish folklore collections (H. F. Feilberg and later surveys).
research_notes: Verified attested: Helhest is a widely documented Danish three-legged death-horse. Description grounded in attested omen and burial traditions; removed unverified 'three hoofprints at Christmas' precision.

description: The Jerff (Gulon, 'Glutton') is a beast described in Olaus Magnus's 'Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus' (1555), a work of northern European natural history and folklore. It was said to be a gluttonous creature that gorged on carrion until its belly swelled, then squeezed between two trees to vomit so it could eat again; likely an exaggerated account of the wolverine (Gulo gulo).
source: Olaus Magnus, 'Historia de Gentibus Septentrionalibus' (1555), northern European bestiary tradition.
research_notes: Verified attested: the gulon/glutton from Olaus Magnus (1555) is genuine, likely based on the wolverine. Description kept close to the historical source; removed speculation about 'medieval Nordic bestiary' moralizing.

description: Aisha Qandisha (Aisha Kandisha) is a female spirit of the Maghreb, most strongly documented in Moroccan folklore but known across the region including Tunisia. Described as a beautiful woman with long hair and lower limbs that end in hooves, she haunts rivers and springs and is said to seduce and harm those who stray; she is invoked in protective rituals and possession practices in North Africa.
source: Maghrebi folklore; documented in Moroccan and Tunisian studies of Aisha Qandisha and related North African spirit-beliefs.
research_notes: Verified attested: Aisha Qandisha is a genuine, well-documented Maghrebi spirit (primary region Morocco, also Tunisia). Description corrected to the attested form (hoofed feet, water association) rather than the vague oasis-beauty portrait in the input.

The entry traces to a single user-generated language-learning wiki page that echoes the input text verbatim. El Jem is the Tunisian town famous for its Roman amphitheater; the serpent is an invented figure, though Tunisian tradition does preserve serpent and jinn lore under other names.

research_notes: Marked unattested/fabricated: 'El Jem' as a serpent appears only in a self-referential user wiki page. Description corrected to state non-attestation and the genuine El Jem (town/amphitheater).

description: El Naddaha ('The Caller') is a female spirit of modern Egyptian folk belief who haunts the banks of the Nile. Described as a woman who calls men to the water at night, she lures them to drown; Egyptian rural tradition treats her as a kind of female jinn, a cautionary figure of riverside danger. The legend spread widely along the Nile in the early twentieth century.
source: Modern Egyptian folk tradition; documented in studies of Nile water-spirit and female-jinn beliefs (the naddaha/caller motif).
research_notes: Verified attested: El Naddaha is a genuine Egyptian riverside caller spirit. Corrected the input's bogus source (Pyramid Texts / Book of the Dead belong to ancient religion, not this modern legend).

description: Abuk is the first woman of Dinka mythology, the one well-known female deity among the Dinka and Nuer (where she is called Buk or Acol). According to the creation myth, Nhialic made Abuk and Garang from clay; Abuk's wish to plant more than the single daily grain led to the separation of heaven and earth. She is the mother of Deng and patroness of women and gardens.
source: Dinka mythology; Britannica (Abuk), Wikipedia (Abuk), Encyclopedia of African Religion.
research_notes: Verified attested: Abuk is a well-documented Dinka first woman/goddess. Description grounded in the attested creation story (planting grain, rope cut); kept core facts.

description: 'Biton' or 'Betón,' poetically called the 'Obsidian Butterfly,' is not attested in Dinka mythology. Its only source is an AI-content site; genuine Dinka tradition has no death spirit of this name or image. The attested Dinka cosmos centers on Nhialic, Deng, Abuk, and Garang, with ancestral Jok spirits and the great serpent Piath.

research_notes: Marked unattested/fabricated: no 'Biton' death spirit in Dinka sources; 'Obsidian Butterfly' is a literary-sounding invention. Description corrected to the attested Dinka pantheon.

description: Aapisowaahs (Apisowaahs, Iipisowaahs) is the Morning Star of Blackfoot tradition, not a Crow figure as the entry claims. He is the son of Nato'si (Sun) and Ko'komiki'somm (Moon); his story, connected to Poia/Star Boy and the Star Bride, is central to Blackfoot star-lore and the Sun Dance. The Crow people have their own cosmology (Old Man Coyote, Akbaatatdia), distinct from this Blackfoot being.
source: Blackfoot oral tradition; native-languages.org (Apisirahts, Morning Star); Blackfoot star-lore collections.
research_notes: Verified attested, but attribution is WRONG: Aapisowaahs is Blackfoot Morning Star (Apisirahts), not Crow. Input conflated Blackfoot deities (Nato'si, Ko'komiki'somm, Apistotoke) with Crow mythology. Description corrected; slug/metadata flagged for re-attribution.

description: Amaguq is the Iñupiaq word for wolf and the name of a wolf-spirit in Inuit tradition, a trickster able to shape-shift between wolf and human form. Reference works on mythological animals record him among Arctic trickster figures, related to the great wolf Amarok. Sources: Yowann Byghan's 'Sacred and Mythological Animals' (2020) and Mary Ellen Snodgrass's 'Encyclopedia of Fable' (1998).
source: Inuit/Iñupiaq tradition; Wikipedia (Amaguq); Byghan, 'Sacred and Mythological Animals' (2020); Snodgrass, 'Encyclopedia of Fable' (1998).
research_notes: Verified attested, thinly: Amaguq is the Iñupiaq wolf/trickster spirit, documented in reference works; related to Amarok. Description grounded in the cited sources; kept attested with fair quality.

description: Bears hold a central place in Haida tradition, appearing as crest figures, on totem poles and regalia, and in the well-known Bear Mother story, in which a woman marries a bear and the bears teach respect for their kind. 'Bear Guardian' is a general label for this attested bear reverence rather than a single named spirit; the boundary between bear and human is a genuine Haida concern.
source: Haida oral tradition and art; documented in studies of Haida crests and the Bear Mother narrative.
research_notes: Kept attested as a synthesis: bear reverence (crests, Bear Mother) is genuinely Haida, but 'Bear Guardian' as a named water-spirit is a label, not an attested being. Description corrected accordingly.

description: Bears are significant in Navajo (Diné) tradition, where they are associated with healing and medicine. The bears figure in the Mountainway, one of the major curing ceremonies, and killing or disrespecting a bear is treated with care. The 'Bear Guardian' is a general label for this attested bear reverence rather than a single named spirit; bear beings appear in curing contexts.
source: Navajo (Diné) tradition; studies of the Mountainway chant and bear-related healing beliefs.
research_notes: Kept attested as a synthesis: bear healing significance and the Mountainway are genuinely Diné; 'Bear Guardian' is a label, not a named being. Corrected the 'western direction' and 'Mountain People' specifics, which overreach the attested record.

The 'bear nature-spirit guarding rivers' framing is a synthesis, not an attested named being; the attested core is Haida reverence for bears.

description: Bears figure among the mythic animal-people of Paiute and Great Basin tradition. Ethnographic sources record Bear as an anthropomorphic animal progenitor of the pre-human age, and Northern Paiute narratives include 'Bear and Fawns.' 'Bear Spirit' is a general label for this attested bear role rather than a single named figure; the central culture heroes are Wolf (Isa) and Coyote.

research_notes: Kept attested as a synthesis: Bear is a documented mythic animal-person of Paiute/Great Basin lore, but the 'bear spirit' is a label, not a named being. Description corrected to the attested animal-people cosmology.

The entry's description even concedes this, framing the 'Bear Trickster' as a composite that does not correspond to any attested Inuit figure. Polar-bear respect is real; this named figure is not.

description: Bears are spiritually significant among the Cree (maskwa), respected as powerful beings and healers in the boreal forest world. The 'Bear Guardian watching over lakes' is a synthesis rather than an attested named figure: Cree tradition centers bears in hunting respect, dreams, and medicine, not specifically as lake spirits. description: Biskinik is the Choctaw 'little news bird,' identified with the yellow-bellied sapsucker. According to Choctaw tradition it was one of two birds (with Folichik, the scissor-tailed flycatcher) to escape the Great Flood, and afterward it served as a friend to the people, tapping messages on trees to warn of approaching visitors and danger. The Choctaw Nation's newspaper bears the bird's name.
source: Choctaw oral tradition; Choctaw Nation publications (Biskinik); Wikipedia (Biskinik); Antrocom journal.
research_notes: Verified attested: Biskinik is a well-documented Choctaw messenger bird (yellow-bellied sapsucker, flood-survivor with Folichik). Description grounded; kept accurate flood detail.
